[The real part is the anticommutator pairing] Since $Bu\in D(A)$ and $Au\in D(B)$, symmetry of $A$ gives $\langle ABu,u\rangle=\langle Bu,Au\rangle=\overline{\langle Au,Bu\rangle}$ and symmetry of $B$ gives $\langle BAu,u\rangle=\langle Au,Bu\rangle$. Adding, $\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}\langle Au,Bu\rangle$. By [F2], $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle Au,Bu\rangle-ab$ with $ab\in\mathbb R$, hence $\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{Re}\langle Au,Bu\rangle-ab=\tfrac12\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle-ab$. Expanding the anticommutator of the centered operators, using $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $\langle Au,u\rangle=a$, $\langle Bu,u\rangle=b$, gives $\langle\{(A-a),(B-b)\}u,u\rangle=\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle-2ab$, so the two displays for the real part agree. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

[The imaginary part is the commutator pairing] By [F2], $\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle=-2i\operatorname{Im}\langle Au,Bu\rangle$; by step 2.1 and [F2], $\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{Im}\langle Au,Bu\rangle$, so $\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle=-2i\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle$. This completes (a). [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

[The two bounds] By [F1] the refined bound $(\Delta A)^{2}(\Delta B)^{2}\ge[\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle]^{2}+[\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle]^{2}$ holds. Substituting step 2.1 and $|\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle|=\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle|$ from step 3.1 gives (c); dropping the nonnegative first square gives (b). [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra]
[Equality] By [F1] equality in the refined bound holds if and only if $x,y$ are linearly dependent; this is (d). [step 4.1, F1]

derivations.claim: [Simple functions commute] Let $f=\sum_{i}a_{i}\mathbf 1_{\Lambda_{i}}$ and $g=\sum_{j}b_{j}\mathbf 1_{\Sigma_{j}}$ be complex simple Borel functions over disjoint measurable covers. By [F1], $f(A)=\sum_{i}a_{i}E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})$ and $g(B)=\sum_{j}b_{j}E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})$, so $$f(A)g(B)=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})=g(B)f(A),$$ because products of scalars commute and each pair of projections commutes by the strong commutation hypothesis. [given, F1, algebra]

[Uniform approximation] Let $f,g$ be bounded Borel and fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F4] choose simple $s,t$ with $\|f-s\|_{\infty}\le\varepsilon$ and $\|g-t\|_{\infty}\le\varepsilon$. By [F1], $\|s(A)-f(A)\|\le\varepsilon$, $\|t(B)-g(B)\|\le\varepsilon$ and $\|t(B)\|\le\|g\|_{\infty}+\varepsilon$, so the operator norm estimate $$\|s(A)t(B)-f(A)g(B)\|\le\|s(A)-f(A)\|\,\|t(B)\|+\|f(A)\|\,\|t(B)-g(B)\|\le\varepsilon\bigl(\|g\|_{\infty}+\varepsilon+\|f\|_{\infty}\bigr)$$ gives $s(A)t(B)\to f(A)g(B)$ in operator norm as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, with the approximants chosen along any sequence $\varepsilon_{n}\to0$. [F1, F4, construct, algebra]

[Clause (a)] Let $f,g$ be bounded Borel and choose the approximating sequences $s_{n}\to f$, $t_{n}\to g$ of step 1.2. By step 1.1, $s_{n}(A)t_{n}(B)=t_{n}(B)s_{n}(A)$ for every $n$; both sides converge in operator norm to $f(A)g(B)$ and to $g(B)f(A)$ respectively by step 1.2 (applied to the pairs $(s_{n},t_{n})$ and $(t_{n},s_{n})$). Limits in operator norm are unique, so $f(A)g(B)=g(B)f(A)$. This is (a). [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, algebra]

[Clause (c), first part] Let $f$ be bounded Borel and let $\Lambda$ be Borel. Applying (a), already proved, to the pair $(f,\mathbf 1_{\Lambda})$ gives $f(B)E_{A}(\Lambda)=E_{A}(\Lambda)f(B)$. This is the first assertion of (c). [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

[Clause (b), membership in the domain] Fix a bounded Borel $f$ and $x\in D(A)$; put $y:=f(B)x$. Put $u_{n}(\lambda):=\lambda\mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}$, so that $A_{n}=\int u_{n}\,dE_{A}$ is a bounded Borel function of $A$; clause (a), already proved, applied to the pair of bounded Borel functions $(u_{n},f)$ gives $A_{n}f(B)=f(B)A_{n}$, so by [F1] and [F3] $$\int\lambda^{2}\mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}\,dE_{A,y}=\|A_{n}y\|^{2}=\|A_{n}f(B)x\|^{2}=\|f(B)A_{n}x\|^{2}\le\|f(B)\|^{2}\|A_{n}x\|^{2}\le\|f(B)\|^{2}\|Ax\|^{2},$$ where the last step uses $\|A_{n}x\|\le\|Ax\|$ for $x\in D(A)$. Letting $n\to\infty$ and using monotone convergence on the left (equivalently the identities of [F3]) gives $\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,y}\le\|f(B)\|^{2}\|Ax\|^{2}<\infty$, so $y\in D(A)$. [step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra]

[Clause (b), action] With $x$ and $y=f(B)x$ as in step 4.1, both $x$ and $y$ lie in $D(A)$. By [F3], $A_{n}x\to Ax$ and $A_{n}y\to Ay$. Using $A_{n}f(B)=f(B)A_{n}$ from step 4.1, $$Ay=\lim_{n}A_{n}y=\lim_{n}A_{n}f(B)x=\lim_{n}f(B)A_{n}x=f(B)Ax,$$ the last equality because $f(B)$ is bounded and $A_{n}x\to Ax$. Hence $Af(B)x=f(B)Ax$ for every $x\in D(A)$. The exchange of roles follows because the strong commutation hypothesis is symmetric in $A$ and $B$, and the extension to bounded linear combinations and norm limits of bounded Borel functions of $B$ follows from linearity and norm continuity of operator multiplication. This proves (b). [step 4.1, F1, F3, algebra]

[Clause (c), composition] Let $f$ be real-valued and bounded Borel and put $F(\Lambda):=E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))$ for Borel $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R$. Preimages preserve the empty set, the whole space, complements and countable unions, so $F$ is a projection-valued measure. For a complex simple $u=\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathbf 1_{D_{i}}$ the preimages $f^{-1}(D_{i})$ are pairwise disjoint, so $\int u\,dF=\sum_{i}c_{i}F(D_{i})=\sum_{i}c_{i}E_{A}(f^{-1}(D_{i}))=\int(u\circ f)\,dE_{A}$; both sides extend to bounded Borel $u$ by the uniform approximation of [F1] and [F4], giving, for every $x\in H$, the scalar identity $\int u\,dF_{x}=\int(u\circ f)\,dE_{A,x}$. Taking $u=u_{n}$ from step 4.1 and letting $n\to\infty$ with monotone convergence gives $\int\lambda^{2}\,dF_{x}=\int f^{2}\,dE_{A,x}=\|f(A)x\|^{2}<\infty$, where the last equality is [F1] for the bounded $f$; and the signed version of the same change of variables gives $\int\lambda\,dF_{x,y}=\int f\,dE_{A,x,y}=\langle f(A)x,y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$. Since $f$ is real-valued, the adjoint-preservation clause of [F2] gives $f(A)^{*}=\Phi_{E_{A}}(\overline f)=\Phi_{E_{A}}(f)=f(A)$, so $f(A)$ is self-adjoint, and $f(A)$ is bounded by [F1]. By the uniqueness of the spectral projection-valued measure of a self-adjoint operator in [F3], $F$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of the bounded self-adjoint operator $f(A)$. By the strong commutation hypothesis, $F(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))=E_{B}(\Sigma)F(\Lambda)$, so $(f(A),B)$ strongly commutes. Applying the same argument once more, now to the pair $(f(A),B)$ and the real-valued bounded Borel function $g$, shows that $(f(A),g(B))$ strongly commutes. This completes (c). [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

This is (ii), including uniqueness. [given, F1, F3, F4]

[(ii) implies (i)] Assume (ii). For Borel $\Lambda,\Sigma$, the multiplicativity [F5] and the marginals give $$E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=G(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)\,G(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)=G(\Lambda\times\Sigma)=G(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)\,G(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(\Lambda),$$ using $(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)\cap(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)=\Lambda\times\Sigma$. [The joint representation] Assume (i)-(iii) and let $G$ be the unique joint projection-valued measure of (ii), so that $G(\Lambda\times\Sigma)=E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)$ for rectangles. Let $W(h):=\int h\,dG$ denote the bounded integral against $G$ for bounded Borel $h:\mathbb R^{2}\to\mathbb C$. [The two product domains] By [F1], $D(Q_{j}P_{j})=\{f:\ P_{j}f\in D(Q_{j})\}=\{f\in D(P_{j}):\ x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}\}$ and $D(P_{j}Q_{j})=\{f:\ Q_{j}f\in D(P_{j})\}=\{f\in D(Q_{j}):\ D_{j}(x_{j}f)\in L^{2}\}$, which are the first two displays of (b).
